elements.name: Adaptor Connector
elements.what: A connector that converts between mismatched interaction policies, interfaces, or data formats of components not designed to interoperate - wrappers, transformers, and protocol converters.
elements.problem: How to compose heterogeneous or independently developed components whose assumptions disagree; conversion cost and semantic fidelity of the mapping are the central forces.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)
elements.borderline: Same NAME family as the design-realm GoF Adapter pattern; the connector type is the architecture-level interaction mediator - both kept per same-name-two-realms rule.

sources_all.src: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Arbitrator Connector
elements.what: A connector that resolves conflicts and redirects control among components with conflicting needs, providing concurrency control (locks, semaphores), scheduling, load balancing, and fault-handling negotiation.
elements.problem: How to coordinate components that contend for shared resources or must agree despite failures; centralizes the coordination policy in the connector instead of scattering it through components.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

sources_all.src: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: AUTOSAR Virtual Function Bus / RTE
elements.what: A communication abstraction in which software components interact through typed ports on a virtual bus, generated per-ECU as the runtime environment (RTE) that maps port communication to intra-ECU calls or network signals.
elements.problem: Component-to-component communication must be independent of deployment; the VFB lets components be designed against logical connections and relocated across ECUs, with the generated RTE realizing each mapping.

elements.name: Data Access Connector
elements.what: A connector through which a component reads or writes data maintained by a data store or another component, covering repository access, database queries, and accessor operations, often with translation/conversion.
elements.problem: How to mediate interaction that flows through persistent or shared state rather than control transfer; transactionality, locality, and format conversion are the governing forces.

sources_all.src: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Distributor Connector
elements.what: A connector that identifies interaction paths and routes communication among components - naming, registration/lookup, and delivery services such as DNS-style naming, routing, and multicast distribution.
elements.problem: How interacting parties find each other and how messages reach them across a topology; never used alone, it composes with procedure-call or stream connectors to form RPCs and distributed messaging.

sources_all.src: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Enterprise Service Bus
elements.what: A shared messaging backbone providing routing, transformation, protocol bridging, and orchestration between enterprise applications.
elements.problem: Point-to-point integration among N systems explodes to N^2 adapters; a mediating bus centralizes translation and routing (and becomes its own coupling point).
elements.named_in: Enterprise Service Bus - Chappell (2004)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Service Bus - Chappell (2004)

elements.name: Event Connector
elements.what: A connector that transfers control and data by delivering occurrences (events) from producers to registered observers, with dimensions for cardinality, delivery guarantees, synchronicity, and notification mode.
elements.problem: How to interact without the initiator knowing or waiting on the recipients; decouples identity and time, but delivery ordering, loss, and causality become connector-level design decisions.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

sources_all.src: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Linkage Connector
elements.what: A connector that ties system elements together by establishing and enforcing associations - name bindings, imports/exports, and compile- or load-time linking - enabling other connectors to act at runtime.
elements.problem: How components come to be composed at all: the facilitation of later interaction; linkage decisions (static vs dynamic, granularity of binding) fix how late a system can be reconfigured.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

sources_all.src: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Message Channel
elements.what: A named logical conduit of the messaging system that senders write messages to and receivers read from.
elements.problem: Applications need addressable, decoupled conduits rather than direct connections to each other.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Procedure Call Connector
elements.what: A connector that transfers control and data between components through invocation with parameters and (usually) a return, spanning local calls, method invocations, callbacks, and system calls.
elements.problem: How to couple components when the caller needs the callee's result before proceeding; the dominant, best-understood interaction primitive, but synchronous and identity-coupled by default.

sources_all.src: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Secure Channel
elements.what: A connector type in which communication between components crosses an authenticated, encrypted transport so confidentiality and integrity hold over untrusted networks.
elements.problem: Data in transit over shared networks can be read and altered; making the channel itself cryptographically protected frees endpoints from trusting the path.

elements.name: Stream Connector
elements.what: A connector that transfers sequences of data between autonomous processes, covering pipes, sockets, and other bounded/unbounded, buffered, structured or raw data flows.
elements.problem: How to move large or continuous data between concurrently executing components; buffering, throughput, ordering, and blocking behavior are the connector's defining choices.

elements.name: Temporal Firewall
elements.what: A unidirectional, time-controlled shared-memory interface between subsystems: the sender deposits temporally accurate state data that the receiver reads at predefined instants, with no control signals crossing the interface in either direction.
elements.problem: Control-flow coupling (interrupts, handshakes) lets timing faults propagate between subsystems; a data-only interface with a priori known access instants blocks error propagation and makes each side independently analyzable.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

elements.name: Time-Triggered Bus
elements.what: A broadcast communication channel whose access is governed by a static TDMA schedule: each node owns pre-assigned slots in a cyclic schedule known to all nodes, so message timing is known a priori.
elements.problem: Contention-based buses make message latency load-dependent and unbounded in the worst case; a static slot schedule gives constant, verifiable latency and doubles as a fault-isolation mechanism (babbling nodes are cut off by bus guardians).
elements.named_in: The Time-Triggered Architecture - Kopetz & Bauer (2003)

sources_all.src: The Time-Triggered Architecture - Kopetz & Bauer (2003)

elements.name: Activator
elements.what: A component that launches services or server processes on demand when a request arrives and can shut them down when idle, instead of keeping every service resident at all times.
elements.problem: Keeping rarely used services running wastes memory and startup capacity, but clients must still be able to reach them at any time; an activation intermediary buys resource economy at the cost of first-request latency.

elements.name: Adapter (container)
elements.what: A sidecar variant that presents a standardized interface (e.g., uniform metrics/log format) over a heterogeneous application to the rest of the system.
elements.problem: Uniform monitoring/management across services built differently, without modifying each service.

elements.name: Ambassador
elements.what: A sidecar variant that proxies the application's outbound connections to the outside world, hiding discovery, sharding, or protocol detail.
elements.problem: Let a component talk to remote dependencies as if local and unsharded; the ambassador absorbs routing/resilience client logic.

elements.name: Auto-Scaling
elements.what: The instance pool grows and shrinks automatically, driven by metrics or schedules evaluated against scaling policies.
elements.problem: Static provisioning wastes capacity at trough and fails at peak; policy-driven elasticity matches deployed capacity to demand without operator action.

elements.name: Blue-Green Deployment
elements.what: Two identical production environments are maintained and releases go live by switching traffic from the active (blue) to the newly deployed (green) environment.
elements.problem: Releasing in place risks downtime and slow rollback; keeping a fully deployed standby environment makes cutover and rollback a routing switch instead of a redeploy.

sources_all.src: Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010); also BlueGreenDeployment - Fowler bliki (2010)

elements.name: Bootloader-Application Split
elements.what: Partitioning firmware into a small, rarely-changed bootloader image and one or more application images in separate flash regions, with the bootloader validating, selecting, updating, and jumping to the application.
elements.problem: Field-updatable devices must survive a failed or interrupted update; keeping an immutable boot stage that can verify images and fall back (golden image, A/B banks) makes the update path recoverable and the root of trust small.

elements.name: Bootloader (boot-stage architecture)
elements.what: A dedicated boot-stage program that initializes the platform, selects/validates an application image, and hands off execution to it.
elements.problem: Field update, image validation and bring-up need a stage that is independent of - and can replace - the application image.
elements.named_in: From Zero to main() series - Memfault (2019)

sources_all.src: From Zero to main() series - Memfault (2019)

elements.name: Canary Release
aka: incremental rollout to a user subset
elements.what: A new version is deployed to a small slice of production servers or users and observed before the rollout is widened to the whole fleet.
elements.problem: Full-fleet releases expose every user to an undetected defect at once; a canary bounds the blast radius and turns release into a monitored experiment.

sources_all.src: Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010); also Site Reliability Engineering - Beyer et al. (2016)

elements.name: Cell-Based Architecture
elements.what: Workload deployed as multiple isolated, self-sufficient instances (cells), each serving a partition of requests, with a thin router directing traffic to cells.
elements.problem: Reduce blast radius: a failure or bad deployment is contained to one cell's share of traffic; fault-isolation bulkheads at workload level.

sources_all.src: Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture - AWS Well-Architected (2023)

elements.name: Container
elements.what: An execution environment that hosts application components and transparently provides them the technical services they need - lifecycle, transactions, security, persistence, resource access - via contracts the components declare.
elements.problem: Domain components should not each reimplement cross-cutting runtime services; hosting them in a managing container buys uniform infrastructure and deploy-time configuration at the cost of conforming to the container's component model. Distinct from OS-level containers (Docker-style isolation), which are a separate deployment element.

elements.name: Compute Resource Consolidation
elements.what: Multiple tasks or operations are consolidated into shared compute units to raise utilization and cut cost.
elements.problem: One deployment unit per small task wastes allocated capacity; packing trades isolation for density.

elements.name: Deployment Pipeline
elements.what: An automated, staged structure through which every change flows from commit to production - build, automated test stages, and deployment stages, each gating promotion of the same artifact.
elements.problem: Manual, ad-hoc release paths make delivery slow and unrepeatable; a single automated pipeline makes the route to production an inspectable, versioned system structure.

elements.name: Deployment Stamps
elements.what: The full solution is replicated as identical scale-unit deployments (stamps), each hosting a subset of tenants/load, with routing in front.
elements.problem: Scale beyond a single deployment's limits and isolate tenants by adding units instead of growing one deployment.

elements.what: Configuration for all application instances is moved to a central external store fetched at startup/run time.
elements.problem: Per-deployment config files diverge across instances and redeploys; centralization gives one managed source.

elements.name: Feature-Flag-Driven Release
elements.what: Code ships to production dark behind runtime toggles, and release becomes a configuration act - enabling the flag for cohorts, rings, or percentages - independent of deployment.
elements.problem: Coupling release to deployment forces long-lived branches and big-bang exposure; runtime toggles let incomplete or risky features ride mainline deploys and be exposed, tested, and killed selectively.

elements.name: Gatekeeper
elements.what: A dedicated hardened host between clients and backends validates and sanitizes all requests, holding no keys or sensitive data itself.
elements.problem: Exposing application hosts directly widens the attack surface; a minimal broker instance absorbs first contact.

elements.name: Geodes
elements.what: Identical active-active deployments distributed across geographic regions, each able to serve any user, backed by globally replicated data.
elements.problem: Serve a global user base with low regional latency and region-loss tolerance, instead of active-passive DR.

elements.name: Immutable Infrastructure
elements.what: Deployed servers/images are never modified in place; every change produces a new image that replaces the old instance wholesale.
elements.problem: In-place patching accumulates configuration drift and snowflake servers; rebuilding from a versioned image makes every environment reproducible and rollback a redeploy of the previous image.

elements.name: Load Balancer
aka: server farm behind a virtual IP
elements.what: An intermediary distributes incoming requests across a pool of equivalent service instances, presenting the pool as one logical endpoint.
elements.problem: A single instance limits capacity and is a single point of failure; a fronting distributor lets capacity scale horizontally and routes around dead instances.

elements.name: OS Container
elements.what: An OS-level isolated execution unit packaging an application with its dependencies, sharing the host kernel, used as the standard unit of deployment and scheduling.
elements.problem: Deployable units need environment-independent packaging and fast, dense isolation without full-VM overhead; containers make the deployment topology reproducible and orchestratable.

elements.what: Instances in a load-balanced pool are replaced with the new version a few at a time, keeping the service up while old and new versions briefly coexist.
elements.problem: Replacing an entire fleet at once requires downtime or double capacity; rolling replacement trades a window of mixed-version operation for zero-downtime upgrades within existing capacity.

elements.name: 4+1 View Model
elements.what: A fixed viewpoint set — logical, process, development, and physical views, plus scenarios (the +1) that tie them together — for describing a software architecture.
elements.problem: Single-diagram architecture descriptions overload one drawing with every stakeholder's concerns; a small fixed set of concurrent views, validated by use-case scenarios, covers the stakeholder spectrum without conflating concerns.

elements.name: Allocation View
elements.what: A view type mapping software elements onto structures in the system's environment — hardware and networks (deployment), file systems (implementation), and teams (work assignment).
elements.problem: Neither module nor runtime structure says where software executes, lives on disk, or who builds it; a dedicated mapping view type carries the software-to-environment correspondences these concerns need.

elements.name: Architectural Perspective
elements.what: A collection of activities, tactics, and guidelines for ensuring that a system exhibits a particular quality property, applied across all of a description's views rather than forming a view of its own.
elements.problem: Quality attributes (security, performance, availability, evolution) cut across every view; treating each as yet another view duplicates content, so a cross-cutting construct is applied to existing views instead. elements.name: Architecture Decision Record
elements.what: A short, versioned document capturing one architecturally significant decision together with its context, status, and consequences.
elements.problem: Design rationale evaporates as teams change; later maintainers see what was decided but not why, and either cargo-cult the decision or blindly reverse it. A lightweight per-decision record kept with the code preserves the why at low cost.

elements.what: A catalog of seven viewpoints — context, functional, information, concurrency, development, deployment, operational — for describing information-system architectures.

elements.what: Data system split into a batch layer (immutable master dataset, recomputed views), a speed layer (incremental real-time views), and a serving layer merging both.

elements.what: Structures a whole system as a hierarchy of abstraction levels in which each layer offers services to the layer above and uses only the layer(s) below.
elements.problem: A large system mixes concerns at very different abstraction levels (hardware access, mechanism, policy, UI); one-way layered dependencies buy exchangeability, portability, and independent evolution at the cost of indirection and pass-through overhead.

elements.name: LMAX Architecture
aka: business logic processor with input/output disruptors
elements.what: A single-threaded in-memory business logic processor is fed and drained by ring-buffer (Disruptor) pipelines, with event sourcing for durability.
elements.problem: Extreme-throughput low-latency processing is defeated by locks and database round-trips; single-writer in-memory design removes both.

elements.name: Main Program and Subroutines
elements.what: A single main program drives the system by calling a hierarchy of subroutines, with control returning up the call tree after each call.
elements.problem: How to organize a computation-dominant system when the decomposition follows functional refinement; correctness of a component depends only on the subroutines it calls, but data flow through shared parameters/globals resists change.

elements.name: MapReduce
elements.what: Batch computation structured as a parallel map phase over partitioned input, a shuffle, and a reduce phase, scheduled across a cluster by a framework.
elements.problem: Run large-scale data processing on commodity clusters while the framework handles partitioning, scheduling, and fault recovery.

elements.name: Message Bus
elements.what: A shared messaging backbone - common channels, a common data model, and a common command set - that all applications plug into to interoperate, joining or leaving without affecting the others.
elements.problem: An enterprise of separate applications must work as one system while letting individual systems be added, removed, or replaced; a common bus buys plug-in interoperability at the cost of enterprise-wide agreement on the shared contract.

elements.name: Messaging
elements.what: Applications integrate by exchanging discrete asynchronous messages over channels provided by a messaging infrastructure, decoupling senders from receivers in time and availability.
elements.problem: Integration must be frequent, immediate-enough, and reliable between systems that cannot assume each other's availability; asynchronous channels buy decoupling and reliability at the cost of eventual consistency and harder end-to-end reasoning.

elements.what: Separates a minimal functional core (fundamental services, communication, extension management) from extended functionality delivered as internal/external servers or plug-ins loaded onto the core.
elements.problem: A platform or product family must adapt to changing requirements and support many variants; keeping the core minimal and pushing features into replaceable extensions buys portability and product-line flexibility at the cost of extra indirection through the core.

elements.what: Client-server generalized to a chain of tiers (e.g. presentation, business logic, data management), each acting as server to the tier before it and client of the tier after it, deployable on separate machines.
elements.problem: How to scale, secure, and independently evolve the presentation, application, and data concerns of an enterprise system; each added tier buys isolation and scaling at the price of latency and deployment complexity.

elements.what: The system is organized as a collection of abstract-data-type instances (objects) that hide their representations and interact by invoking each other's operations.
elements.problem: How to localize the effects of representation change; encapsulation lets internals evolve freely, at the cost that every caller must know the identity of the object it invokes.

elements.what: Networked components (peers) act as both clients and servers of one another, discovering and exchanging services directly without a distinguished central server.
elements.problem: How to achieve scalability, resilience, and resource pooling when no node can be trusted or provisioned as a permanent center; pays for decentralization with discovery, consistency, and trust problems.

elements.what: Organizes a processing system as a chain of independent filter components connected by pipes that carry a data stream from source to sink.
elements.problem: A whole processing task must be decomposable, recombination-friendly, and incrementally streamable; independent filters buy reuse, reordering, and parallel deployment at the cost of shared-format agreement and per-stage transfer overhead. elements.what: The system is organized around a control loop: a controller reads process variables from sensors, compares them to set points, and adjusts manipulated variables to keep a physical or continuing process on target.
elements.problem: How to maintain specified properties of an ongoing process in the face of external disturbances that cannot be predicted, using open- vs closed-loop and feedback vs feedforward variants; the architecture must make the loop, not the call graph, the primary structure.

elements.problem: Communication concerns (framing, routing, reliability, sessions) must evolve independently; strict layering with encapsulation isolates them.

elements.what: A hybrid network-based style constraining client-server interaction to be stateless, cacheable, layered, and mediated by a uniform interface over resources identified by URIs and manipulated via exchanged representations, optionally extended by code-on-demand.
elements.problem: How to make an Internet-scale hypermedia system evolvable, scalable, and visible to intermediaries; the constraints trade per-interaction efficiency (self-descriptive messages, statelessness) for anarchic scalability and independent deployment of components.

elements.name: RTOS-Based Architecture
elements.what: A whole-system structure in which the application is decomposed into prioritized, preemptively scheduled RTOS tasks communicating through kernel objects (queues, semaphores, events), with response times set by priority rather than loop position.
elements.problem: When response requirements differ by orders of magnitude across activities, cooperative loops cannot bound latency for the urgent ones; a preemptive kernel decouples each activity's worst-case response from the rest of the system.

elements.name: Rule-Based System
elements.what: An interpreter specialization in which a rule engine (inference/interpretation engine) selects and fires condition-action rules from a knowledge base against working memory.
elements.problem: How to keep volatile domain logic out of code so domain experts can evolve behavior as rules; control flow becomes emergent from rule selection rather than explicit.

elements.name: SEDA (Staged Event-Driven Architecture)
elements.what: Service structured as a network of event-driven stages connected by explicit queues, each stage with its own thread pool and admission control.
elements.problem: Well-conditioned behavior under massive load: per-stage queues give backpressure points and prevent overcommit that thread-per-request designs suffer.

elements.what: An embedded-systems organization structured as a repeating loop of sensor reading, computation over the sensed values plus internal state, and actuator commands controlling the environment.
elements.problem: How to structure reactive embedded software whose primary job is continuous interaction with physical hardware; keeps timing and I/O concerns explicit at the top level rather than buried in a call hierarchy.

elements.what: Processing units with replicated in-memory data grids, synchronized asynchronously to persistent storage, so the database is out of the request path.
elements.problem: Extreme/variable concurrency where the database is the bottleneck; achieves elastic scale by removing the central data store from the hot path.

elements.what: A whole reactive system is organized as a set of states plus named transitions that move the system between them, making the state machine the top-level structure rather than an internal mechanism.
elements.problem: How to give reactive/real-time systems an analyzable top-level structure whose behavior can be enumerated and verified; differs from an in-component FSM by governing system organization, not one module's logic.

elements.what: Structures data processing as a long-running dataflow graph over unbounded streams with windowing, watermarks and triggers.
elements.problem: Unbounded, out-of-order data cannot be handled by batch topologies; the streaming model trades off correctness, latency and cost explicitly.

elements.what: Layers of behavior-producing modules run concurrently, with higher layers subsuming (suppressing/overriding) the outputs of lower ones instead of a central planner.
elements.problem: Robot control needs robust real-time reaction without a monolithic sense-plan-act pipeline; layered competence levels degrade gracefully and are incrementally buildable.

elements.name: Superloop Architecture
elements.what: A whole-system structure with no operating system: one endless main loop polls and services every task in turn, optionally with interrupts as the foreground layer feeding flags/buffers to the background loop.
elements.problem: Small systems cannot afford an RTOS's footprint and complexity; a single statically ordered loop gives minimal overhead and full determinism of structure, at the cost of coarse timing control and poor scalability.

elements.what: System-level organization in which all communication and computation are driven by the progression of a fault-tolerant global time base, with statically planned activation instants known a priori at all nodes.
elements.problem: Distributed hard real-time systems need temporal predictability, composability, and fault isolation; event-driven activation makes worst-case behavior and certification arguments hard, while a global static schedule makes temporal behavior verifiable by construction.

elements.what: Provide redundant components that are diverse not only internally but also in their inputs and outputs (e.g. computing aircraft altitude by barometric pressure, radar, and geometry), with a sophisticated blending/voting mechanism.

elements.what: Record user and system actions and their effects so an attacker's actions can be traced and identified, supporting prosecution and improved future defenses.

elements.what: Ensure an authenticated actor has the rights to access and modify data or services, via access control mechanisms assigned per actor, actor class, or role.

elements.name: Bound Execution Times
elements.what: Place a limit on how much execution time is used to respond to an event — e.g. bounding iteration counts in data-dependent iterative algorithms — trading computational accuracy for bounded latency.
elements.problem: Unbounded computations make response time unpredictable; often paired with Manage Sampling Rate, and requires assessing whether the less-accurate result is good enough.

elements.name: Bound Queue Sizes
elements.what: Control the maximum number of queued arrivals, and thereby the resources used to process them, with an explicit policy for what happens when queues overflow.
elements.problem: Unbounded queues consume unbounded resources and hide overload; bounding them forces a deliberate overflow/loss policy, usually paired with Limit Event Response.

elements.name: Cancel
elements.what: Support user-issued cancellation: a listener not blocked by the operation being cancelled, termination of the activity, release of its resources, and notification of collaborating components so they act appropriately.
elements.problem: Users must be able to stop an in-progress operation; naive designs block the cancel path behind the very operation to be cancelled and leak its resources.

elements.name: Condition Monitoring
elements.what: Check conditions in a process or device, or validate assumptions made during design (e.g. by computing checksums), to prevent the system from producing faulty behavior.
elements.problem: A system can drift outside its assumed operating conditions without any single operation failing; the monitor itself must be simple enough not to introduce new faults.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Configure Behavior
elements.what: Build components so their behavior can be configured — during build, deployment/startup, or runtime — to operate in the modes an integrating system expects.
elements.problem: A component with a single fixed behavior fits only one integration context; configurability lets one implementation satisfy many.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Defense in Depth
elements.what: Multiple independent security controls are layered along the path to an asset so that compromising any single control does not compromise the system.
elements.problem: Any single control can fail or be bypassed; stacking heterogeneous barriers forces an attacker to defeat several mechanisms and buys detection time.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006); also NIST SP 800-53 usage
elements.borderline: Principle-flavored, admitted as the structural layering of independent controls (bridge endpoint for validation, authN/Z, and isolation design elements).

elements.name: Defer Binding
elements.what: Bind values and choices as late in the life cycle as cost-effective: at compile/build time (component replacement, compile-time parameterization, aspects), at deployment/startup (configuration-time binding, resource files), or at runtime (discovery, interpreted parameters, shared repositories, polymorphism).
elements.problem: Human-mediated change is costly and error-prone; building in flexibility lets computers effect the change, trading up-front mechanism cost against per-change cost and enabling change by non-developers ('externalizing' change).
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Degradation
elements.what: In the presence of component failures, maintain the most critical system functions while dropping or substituting less critical ones in a planned, deliberate, safe way.
elements.problem: Individual component failures should reduce system functionality gracefully rather than cause total collapse; e.g. a navigation system falling back to dead reckoning in a tunnel.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Detect Intrusion
elements.what: Compare network traffic or service request patterns within a system against a database of signatures or known patterns of malicious behavior (protocol, payload size, source/destination address, port).
elements.problem: Attacks in progress must be recognized among legitimate traffic before the system can react.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Detect Message Delay
elements.what: Detect potential man-in-the-middle attacks by checking the time taken to deliver or receive messages against normally stable delivery times, and by watching for anomalous connect/disconnect counts.
elements.problem: An interceptor that reads or modifies messages in transit adds latency and connection churn that timing analysis can expose.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Detect Service Denial
elements.what: Compare the pattern or signature of incoming network traffic against historical profiles of known denial-of-service attacks.
elements.problem: Denial-of-service traffic must be distinguished from legitimate load spikes before countermeasures can be applied.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Discover
elements.what: Match service requests to service providers at runtime through a discovery service, enabling identification and remote invocation of providers that were not bound at build time; in the energy context, requests can be annotated so providers are selected by energy characteristics.
elements.problem: Statically bound providers cannot be swapped or selected by runtime criteria (location, version, energy cost); a discovery mechanism defers and mediates the binding.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Dynamic Classification
elements.what: Estimate energy consumption with a dynamic model — a table lookup, a regression over past executions, or a simulation — that accounts for transient conditions such as workload.
elements.problem: Static energy models are insufficient when consumption depends heavily on runtime conditions.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Encapsulate
elements.what: Introduce an explicit interface to an element and hide its internals so that other elements depend only on the interface, reducing the strength of coupling and the syntactic/semantic distance to be bridged.
elements.problem: Direct dependence on an element's internals means every internal change and every integration must confront those internals; an interface localizes the dependency.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Encrypt Data
elements.what: Apply encryption (symmetric or asymmetric) to stored data and to communication, providing confidentiality beyond authorization controls — and the sole protection on links that have none.
elements.problem: Data at rest and in transit can be read by parties outside the authorization perimeter; encryption makes possession without keys useless.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Escalating Restart
elements.what: Recover by restarting components at progressively coarser granularity levels (e.g. child threads only, then unprotected memory, then all memory, then full image reload), choosing the least disruptive level that clears the fault.
elements.problem: A full restart is maximally disruptive; matching the restart granularity to the fault minimizes the impact on service, supporting graceful degradation.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Exception Detection
elements.what: Detect system conditions that alter the normal flow of execution, refined by the book into system exceptions, parameter fence, parameter typing, and timeout.
elements.problem: Faults such as divide-by-zero, bus/address faults, illegal instructions, or violated timing constraints must be turned into detectable events rather than silent corruption.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Exception Handling
elements.what: After an exception is detected, handle it using mechanisms ranging from function return codes to exception classes carrying name, origin, and cause, so the fault can be masked or repaired.
elements.problem: Simply crashing on a detected exception is unacceptable for availability; the system needs structured information and a place to act on it.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Exception Prevention
elements.what: Employ techniques that keep exceptions from arising at all — error-correcting codes, abstract data types such as smart pointers, and wrappers that preclude dangling pointers or semaphore access violations.
elements.problem: Whole fault classes (resource leaks, out-of-bounds access) can be excluded by construction more cheaply than detecting and recovering from them.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Executable Assertions
elements.what: Hand-code assertions checking that data values satisfy specified constraints — placed wherever the data is referenced or modified, expressible as method pre/postconditions or class invariants — so the program flags when and where it enters a faulty state.
elements.problem: Faulty states can pass silently through execution; systematically placed assertions embed the test oracle in the code, increasing observability.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Failover
elements.what: On failure of an active unit, service is switched to a redundant standby unit that assumes its role.
elements.problem: Continuity of service across unit failures requires a designated takeover path and role reassignment.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

sources_all.src: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Feature Toggle
elements.what: Integrate a runtime 'kill switch' for new features so a deployed feature can be automatically disabled without initiating a new deployment.
elements.problem: Even fully tested features can misbehave after deployment; controlling them without the cost and risk of redeploying requires a toggle mechanism in the architecture.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Heartbeat
elements.what: A monitored component periodically emits a message to (or resets a watchdog timer in) a system monitor, so that the absence of the heartbeat signals failure.
elements.problem: Failure of a component must be detected without the monitor having to actively probe it; the component itself takes the initiative to demonstrate liveness.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Identify Actors
elements.what: Identify the source of any external input to the system — users by user IDs; other systems by access codes, IP addresses, protocols, or ports.
elements.problem: Authentication and authorization presuppose knowing which actor an input claims to come from.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Ignore Faulty Behavior
elements.what: Ignore messages from a particular source once they are determined to be spurious, e.g. messages from a sensor known to have failed.
elements.problem: A faulty component can flood the system with bogus events; continuing to act on them propagates the fault.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Increase Competence Set
elements.what: Design a component to handle more cases — states that would otherwise be faults — as part of its normal operation, e.g. waiting or returning gracefully when a resource is blocked instead of throwing.
elements.problem: A component throws an exception when it finds itself outside the set of states it is competent to handle; enlarging that set converts faults into handled situations.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Increase Resource Usage Efficiency
elements.what: Improve the efficiency of the algorithms used in critical areas to decrease latency and improve throughput and resource consumption.
elements.problem: Inefficient critical-path algorithms consume resources that better algorithms would free; 'optimizing the code' is one tactic among many, not the only lever.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Increase Resources
elements.what: Add or upgrade resources — faster processors, additional processors, more memory, faster networks — to improve performance.
elements.problem: When demand cannot be reduced, capacity must grow; despite its cost, adding resources is often the cheapest immediate route to better performance.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Inform Actors
elements.what: When the system detects an attack, notify the relevant set of actors — operators, other personnel, or cooperating systems — so they can act.
elements.problem: An ongoing attack may require human or cross-system action that the detecting system cannot take alone.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Interlock
elements.what: Protect against failures arising from incorrect event ordering by controlling all access to protected components, including enforcing the correct sequencing of events affecting them.
elements.problem: Some hazards arise not from wrong values but from right actions in the wrong order; an interlock makes illegal orderings impossible.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Introduce Concurrency
elements.what: Process requests in parallel — different event streams on different threads, or additional threads for different activity sets — to reduce blocked time, then choose a scheduling policy via Schedule Resources.
elements.problem: Serialized processing leaves requests blocked behind one another even when independent; concurrency reclaims that waiting time.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Access
elements.what: Restrict access to computing resources by limiting the number of access points and/or the types of traffic allowed through them — e.g. a demilitarized zone between internet and intranet bounded by a pair of firewalls.
elements.problem: Every access point and permitted traffic type enlarges the attack surface; minimizing both contains exposure.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Event Response
elements.what: Process events only up to a set maximum rate, queueing or deliberately dropping events that arrive faster, triggered by queue size, processor utilization, or SLA violation.
elements.problem: Bursts beyond processing capacity force a policy choice: guarantee no loss (size queues for the worst case) or drop events (and decide whether to log or notify).
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Exposure
elements.what: Minimize the damage a successful attack can do by reducing the amount of data or services reachable through any single access point — a passive defense that compartmentalizes value.
elements.problem: If one breached access point yields everything, every breach is catastrophic; spreading assets bounds per-attack loss.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Nondeterminism
elements.what: Find and, where possible, eliminate sources of behavioral nondeterminism such as unconstrained parallelism; where unavoidable (e.g. multithreaded response to unpredictable events), manage it with tactics like record/playback.
elements.problem: Nondeterministic systems are pernicious to test because failures do not reproduce; determinism restores repeatability.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Limit Structural Complexity
elements.what: Keep the structure simple enough to test: avoid or resolve cyclic dependencies, isolate and encapsulate environmental dependencies, reduce inter-component coupling, constrain inheritance depth/fan-out and polymorphism, and track metrics such as response-of-class, propagation cost, and decoupling level.
elements.problem: Large operational state spaces make recreating an exact state — and thus reproducing failures — hard; high cohesion, loose coupling, and separation of concerns shrink the state space.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Localize State Storage
elements.what: Store system/subsystem/component state in a single place — conveniently a state machine object tracking and reporting the current state — so tests can start the system in any desired state, at whatever granularity testing needs.
elements.problem: Hidden or scattered state makes starting a test from an arbitrary known state difficult or impossible.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain Multiple Copies of Computations
elements.what: Run multiple replicas of a computation (replicated services in a microservice architecture, replicated web servers in a pool) with a load balancer assigning new work among them.
elements.problem: Funneling all service requests through a single instance creates contention; replicas spread the load.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain Multiple Copies of Data
elements.what: Keep copies of data — replication (separate identical copies to reduce contention) or caching (copies, possibly subsets, on storage with different access speeds, possibly predictively prefetched) — accepting the burden of keeping copies consistent.
elements.problem: Simultaneous access to one copy of data creates contention, and distant/slow storage adds latency; copies trade consistency-maintenance work for reduced contention and faster access.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain System Model
elements.what: The system maintains an explicit model of itself to determine expected system behavior and give users appropriate feedback — the progress bar predicting time to completion is the canonical manifestation.
elements.problem: Users need feedback about what the system is doing and how long it will take; producing it requires the system to model its own behavior.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain Task Model
elements.what: Maintain a model of the task the user is performing so the system can infer context and assist — e.g. predictive type-ahead in search engines, spell correction in mail clients.
elements.problem: System-initiated help requires knowing what the user is trying to do; without a task model the system cannot anticipate.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Maintain User Model
elements.what: Maintain an explicit model of a user or user class — their knowledge of the system, expected response-time behavior, error patterns — updated dynamically or offline; user-interface customization is a special case where users edit the model directly.
elements.problem: One-size-fits-all interaction ignores what individual users know and need; encapsulating the model makes tailoring and modification easy.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Manage Event Arrival
elements.what: Control the arrival rate of events from external systems, canonically by setting a service level agreement that fixes the maximum event rate the system will support, constraining both system and clients.
elements.problem: Demand beyond the sustainable arrival rate degrades everyone's response time; capping arrivals makes load explicit and pushes overflow to additional instances.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Manage Resources (Integrability)
elements.what: Interpose an explicit resource manager that mediates access to shared computing resources (memory, threads, hardware devices) so independently developed components can share them safely.
elements.problem: Components that each assume exclusive resource ownership conflict when integrated; a mediator arbitrates. (Named 'Manage Resources' in bck's integrability chapter; not to be confused with the performance category of the same name.)
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Manage Sampling Rate
elements.what: Reduce (possibly dynamically) the frequency at which environmental input is sampled — sensor data rates, video frames per second — trading fidelity for predictable latency.
elements.problem: When the system cannot keep up with the incoming data stream, lower-fidelity but stable processing may beat unstable latency; common in signal-processing systems.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Manage Service Interactions
elements.what: Allow multiple versions of system services to be deployed and executed simultaneously, with client requests routed to any version, coordinating inter-service interactions to proactively avoid version incompatibilities.
elements.problem: Simultaneously running old and new versions avoids fully duplicating resources during upgrade but introduces version-compatibility hazards that must be managed.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Masking
elements.what: Mask a fault by comparing the results of several redundant components and using a voting procedure when they differ, so the faulty result never propagates; requires a simple, highly reliable voter.
elements.problem: Some systems must keep producing correct outputs through component faults, not merely detect them; masking hides the fault behind redundancy.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Metering
elements.what: Collect data about the energy consumption of computing resources in near real time via a sensor infrastructure — from data-center meters down to metered rack PDUs, ASICs, or battery management systems.
elements.problem: Energy cannot be managed without being measured; different granularities of measurement need different instrumentation.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Monitor
elements.what: A dedicated component monitors the health of other parts of the system (processors, processes, I/O, memory) and coordinates the other fault-detection tactics.
elements.problem: Faults must be observed by some part of the system before any repair can begin; a system needs a designated observer to detect failures or congestion, e.g. denial-of-service conditions.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Non-Stop Forwarding
elements.what: Split functionality into a control/management plane and a data plane so that when the control plane fails, the data plane keeps forwarding along known routes while routing information is rebuilt and validated.
elements.problem: In router-like systems, supervisory failure should not stop the ongoing data-moving work; the concept originates in router design.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Nonrepudiation
elements.what: Guarantee that the sender of a message cannot later deny sending it and the receiver cannot deny receiving it, via some combination of digital signatures and trusted third-party certification.
elements.problem: Transactions between mutually distrustful parties need binding evidence of send and receipt.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Orchestrate
elements.what: Introduce a control mechanism (e.g. an orchestration engine or workflow controller) that coordinates, sequences, and invokes otherwise independent services so they work together.
elements.problem: Independently developed services have no shared control flow; centralizing coordination keeps the integration logic out of the services themselves.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Package Dependencies
elements.what: Package an element together with its dependencies (libraries, OS version, utility containers) — via containers, pods, or virtual machines — so they deploy together and dependency versions stay consistent from development to production.
elements.problem: An element that behaves correctly in development can fail in production when the surrounding dependency versions differ.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Parameter Fence
elements.what: Place a known data pattern immediately after any variable-length parameters of an object so that overwrites of that memory can be detected at runtime.
elements.problem: Buffer overruns into memory allocated for variable-length parameters are otherwise silent until they corrupt unrelated state.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Parameter Typing
elements.what: Use a base class defining functions to add, find, and iterate over type-length-value (TLV) message parameters so that sender and receiver agree on content types and disagreements are detected.
elements.problem: Untyped message payloads let sender and receiver silently disagree about the meaning of bytes on the wire.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)
elements.borderline: Implementation-flavored like parameter fence, but named as an availability sub-tactic in bck; kept per over-inclusion rule.

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Pause/Resume
elements.what: Let users pause and later resume long-running operations (e.g. large downloads), temporarily freeing resources for reallocation to other tasks.
elements.problem: Long-running operations monopolize resources and user attention; suspension without loss of progress restores control to the user.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Ping/Echo
elements.what: Nodes exchange asynchronous request/response message pairs to determine reachability and round-trip delay, with a time threshold before the pinged component is declared failed.
elements.problem: A monitor must determine whether a remote component is alive and reachable over a network path, and how long the path takes.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Predictive Model
elements.what: Combine a model with monitoring to predict, from operational metrics (session establishment rates, threshold crossings, process-state and queue-length statistics), that a fault or unsafe condition is approaching, and take corrective action early.
elements.problem: Waiting for faults to occur before reacting is too late for high-availability and safety-critical operation; early warning enables preemptive correction.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Prioritize Events
elements.what: Impose a priority scheme ordering events by importance of servicing them, so that under resource pressure low-priority events may be ignored at minimal cost.
elements.problem: Not all events are equally important (a fire alarm vs. a room-temperature notice); treating them uniformly wastes resources on the unimportant under load.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
elements.what: A queue is placed between producers and a service so bursts are absorbed by the queue and the service consumes at its sustainable rate.
elements.problem: Intermittent heavy load overwhelms downstream services provisioned for average demand; the buffer converts bursts into throughput-bounded work.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Queue-Based Load Leveling - Azure Architecture Center (living)

elements.name: Reconfiguration
elements.what: Recover from failure by reassigning responsibilities — remapping the logical architecture onto the (possibly limited) resources or components still functioning — while preserving as much functionality as possible.
elements.problem: After failures the remaining resources differ from the planned deployment; the system must keep operating on what is left, possibly combined with degradation.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Record/Playback
elements.what: Record information as it crosses interfaces and use the recorded state to 'play the system back', recreating the fault-inducing state as input to further tests.
elements.problem: The state that causes a failure is often hard to recreate manually; capturing it at interfaces makes failures reproducible, including in nondeterministic systems.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Redistribute Responsibilities
elements.what: Move similar responsibilities scattered across several modules into one module (existing or new), guided by change scenarios showing which responsibilities move together.
elements.problem: When one likely change touches many modules, or a module contains parts untouched by any scenario, responsibilities are misallocated and change cost multiplies.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Reduce Computational Overhead
elements.what: Reduce the work spent per event by removing costly indirection (while ideally preserving encapsulation through code optimization or proxy-established direct communication), co-locating communicating components (same processor, same runtime, same rack), and periodically cleaning inefficient-grown resources such as hash tables and virtual memory maps.
elements.problem: Intermediaries and separation of concerns — valuable for modifiability — add per-event processing and communication cost; this is the classic modifiability/performance trade-off.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Reduce Usage
elements.what: Reduce energy use by device-level actions (lower refresh rate, dim display), removing or deactivating unneeded resources (spin down disks, power off CPUs/servers, reduce clock rate), consolidating VMs onto fewer physical servers, or offloading computation to the cloud.
elements.problem: Resources kept powered beyond demand waste energy; usage must track need.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

sources_all.src: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Redundant Spare
elements.what: Configure one or more spare components that can step in and take over when an active component fails; hot/warm/cold variants differ in how current the spare's state is at takeover.
elements.problem: A failed active component must be replaced quickly to keep the service available; the trade-off is between resource cost of keeping spares synchronized and recovery time.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)
